scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance and tune emerged in the early 1850s as a variation of 'The Haymakers', a jig dating back to the 18th century.
By December 1852, it became a fashionable social dance in the United Kingdom, championed by dance-masters like Eugène Coulon and featured at court balls.
Sheet music was published in London and America in 1853.
on_screen: Map: United Kingdom · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally performed at fashionable social balls, private parties, and theatrical stages, later becoming a children's playground game.
The title phrase has inspired numerous interpretations, including spinner's weaver gears, tailor's tools, and Cockney rhyming slang for pawning a coat.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in two parallel lines of couples.

Figures include balancing (Ballaneez), galloping down the inside and back, taking hands in circles with neighboring partners, and passing a partner under raised arms while the group sings the refrain 'pop goes the weasel'.
In the later children's game variant, participants circle around rings and scramble for spots when the song reaches the pop refrain.
Watch for Passing under arms.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Built upon a traditional jig rhythm, predominantly in 6/8 meter with an animated tempo.
Historical instruments include fiddles, pianos, guitars, and mechanical street hand-organs.
Listen for the fiddle, piano, guitar, hand-organs.
The pulse is 6/8.
A lively, bouncing jig melody driven by rhythmic string or keyboard instrumentation that builds in energy before concluding with a sudden, pronounced vocal or mechanical pop.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Eugène Coulon introduced the fashionable dance-master choreography to court balls.
James W. Porter arranged American sheet music variants.
British versions reference local London landmarks such as City Road and the Eagle pub, as well as tuppenny rice and treacle.
